sentences.text: I wanted the feet.
That evening I scattered flour across the hut floor, from the bed to the door.
I did not chain my ankle.
I lay down in my clothes with my eyes open as long as I could keep them.
In the morning the flour had a path in it.
Bare feet, the second toe longer than the first.
From the bed to the door.
The door was latched from outside.
I followed the prints along the crown of the road on my knees.
Every fifth step they leaned a little to the left, as if someone were walking with a hand held out.
They reached the post and stopped, facing the village.
Then more prints.
Boots, a ring of them, around mine.
They had not trodden on one print of mine.
I sat on the wet stone and let it be true.
She walks barefoot every night, and the flood tide takes her prints before I wake.
The small bare prints in the atlas.
They were mine.
But a woman who finds her child on a closing road carries her home and shuts the door.
Her heels did not go home.
I could not make that sentence add up, so I put it aside.
I went back to the rope, because a rope remembers.
Under the bright groove of my own left hand there was another.
Older.
Deeper.
Higher up the rope, at the reach of a taller woman.
And worked into the strands, grey wool.
I knew only one coat that colour.
